title: Claude Code: Auto Mode, Hierarchical Subagents & Dynamic Workflows (2026)
content:
## Overview

Through 2026, Claude Code's headline additions have moved past single-agent editing toward managed autonomy: agents that supervise their own permission decisions, agents that spawn other agents multiple levels deep, and a planner that fans out hundreds of subagents in one session. This page covers the features that shipped after the original Claude Code overview page was written.

---

## Auto Mode

Auto mode replaces per-action permission prompts with a background safety classifier: safe tool calls proceed uninterrupted, while risky ones (e.g., destructive git operations, broad file deletion) are still blocked or escalated for approval. Initially a research preview, auto mode has since expanded to Pro accounts and is now the default on Bedrock, Vertex AI, and Foundry deployments as of July 2026, running on both Sonnet 4.6 and Opus-tier models.

Auto mode's classifier evaluates subagents at multiple points: at spawn time (checking the delegated task description before the subagent starts — e.g. blocking "delete all remote branches matching this pattern" before it executes), and during execution (checking each tool call the subagent makes). When a parent session runs in auto mode, its subagents inherit auto mode automatically, and any `permissionMode` set in a subagent's own frontmatter is ignored in favor of the parent's rules.

---

## Hierarchical Subagents

As of Claude Code v2.1.172, subagents are no longer a single flat layer — a subagent can spawn its own child subagents, up to three levels deep. This lets a task decompose recursively instead of routing everything back through the top-level coordinator.

The canonical example: a **reviewer** subagent reads a diff and produces a list of findings, then — instead of grading its own work — dispatches a separate **verifier** subagent per finding to check it adversarially. Only the reviewer's final, verified summary surfaces to the main conversation; the intermediate verifier chatter stays contained. This mirrors the adversarial-verification pattern used in Workflow scripts, but now available directly through ad hoc subagent spawning.

---

## Dynamic Workflows (Opus 4.8, research preview)

Shipped alongside Claude Opus 4.8 (May 28, 2026), dynamic workflows let Claude plan a large body of work up front and then execute it by running **hundreds of parallel subagents in a single Claude Code session**, rather than working through files or modules serially. This targets tasks like large-scale migrations or repo-wide refactors where the bottleneck was previously the coordinator manually re-invoking subagents one batch at a time.

---

## Other Notable Additions

- **`/doctor`** — a full setup-health checkup: verifies installation integrity, and flags unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins that are costing context budget without being used.
- **`fallbackModel`** — a configurable chain of backup models so a session degrades gracefully (rather than failing) if a primary model is unavailable or rate-limited.
- **Community tool marketplace** — a discovery surface for sharing and installing third-party tools/plugins, extending the existing `.claude/agents/` and `.claude/commands/` customization model.
- **`/loop`** — runs an automated cycle (e.g., run tests → fix → re-run) until a condition is met (such as a fully green test suite), without requiring manual confirmation at every step. Well suited to large refactors and migrations.
- **Claude in Chrome (GA, July 2026)** — browser-based Claude Code integration reached general availability, alongside Sonnet 5 becoming Claude Code's default model.

---

## Why This Matters

The throughline across these features is reducing human-in-the-loop friction for large or long-horizon tasks: auto mode removes prompt-by-prompt gatekeeping for safe actions, hierarchical subagents let decomposition happen recursively instead of funneling through one coordinator, and dynamic workflows push parallelism from a handful of subagents to hundreds. Together they shift Claude Code from "pair programmer" toward something closer to a supervised engineering team.
